name: Islamic fundamentalism
summary: Islamic fundamentalism seeks a return to the original texts of Islam, the Quran and Sunnah, and the application of sharia as the basis of law and public life. Its adherents reject the separation of religion and state, secular democracy and Western cultural influence, and hold that sovereignty belongs to God alone. Strands differ on whether change should come by preaching, elections or armed jihad.
scope: Islamic fundamentalism as the defining sources describe it: the Muslim current that holds the Quran and Sunnah to give rules for all of social, political and economic life, presents Islam as a comprehensive system distinct from every other, and rejects Westernising modernists, secularists and nationalists (Shepard; Britannica). The core is the Sunni lay-revivalist line of Hasan al-Banna and the Muslim Brotherhood and Abul A'la Mawdudi (with Qutb's Milestones as a text the sources place in the same current), read as a text-first, sharia-first programme. Britannica also files Wahhabism, Salafism, the Taliban, Boko Haram and Iran's Principlists under the label and notes they differ widely (some use terrorism, some do not; some leftist, some free-market); those strands, Shi'i clerical rule and the Gulf monarchies' state religion are not represented here. Modernist Islam is excluded.

ban-interest.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) lists the prohibition of interest among the explicit Qur'anic laws and as a divine limit on economic life.

clerical-rule.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 4) says Islamic theocracy "is not ruled by any particular religious class but by the whole community of Muslims", and calls a priestly class ruling in God's name "satanic rather than divine".

consent-of-governed.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 4) bases the ruler's authority on the delegated vicegerency of the community, which can hold him to account.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Qutb's Milestones sets Islam against Jahiliyyah and holds the Islamic way superior to every other.

death-penalty.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) defends the Shari'ah penalties, including stoning for adultery by the married, and discusses commuting death sentences.

democracy-best.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 4) says Islam and Western democracy as a philosophy "are basically different, rather opposed", since sovereignty belongs to God, though Islam has its own democratic form of organisation. The statement's "even when voters choose badly" cannot stand against Shari'ah limits.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) says the Divine limits remove "class war ... which begins with capitalist oppression and ends in working-class dictatorship"; he rejects communism and dictatorship.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 10) says active politics and administration are not the field of women and proposes a women-only body for women's affairs; Purdah puts the man in charge of the family as provider and protector.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 4) teaches that sovereignty belongs to God alone; Qutb's Milestones holds the same of Allah's authority.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (intro) calls monarchy and despotism "institutions alien to the letter and spirit" of Islam.

elective-rulers.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 4) has the head of state chosen by the Muslim community's vicegerency and answerable to it; a ruler who turns himself into a dictator is a usurper.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 5) says disparities of wealth "are not necessarily unnatural" and that "equality of the unequals is no equality".

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 10) rejects women sitting in the legislative assemblies; any women's body would be confined to women, elected by women, for women's affairs.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Purdah calls the Western doctrine of equal sex roles a "wrong concept of equality" that makes women forget their "natural functions", treating the roles as set by nature.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) holds that Western secularism and its political forms do not suit Muslims, for whom the Islamic state is "the natural movement of their history".

islam-incompatible.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 4 note) calls Islam and Western democracy as philosophies "basically different, rather opposed"; Qutb's Milestones sets Islam against the Jahili West.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (chs. 1-2) makes the Qur'an and Sunnah the supreme law no legislature may overstep; Qutb's Milestones makes Allah's law the only legitimate rule.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) lists "the prohibition of use of intoxicants in general" among the principles the law must carry; adults' recreational drug use is not left free.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) names the Qur'anic punishment for adultery among laws of the state; Purdah has a section "Punishment for Fornication". Consensual sex outside marriage is a punishable offence, not legal.

more-religion-public.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) holds the state must be run on divine law and rejects separating politics from religion and morality; Islamic Way of Life treats Islam as covering all of life.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) rejects both capitalist oppression and communist dictatorship; Qutb's Milestones calls both systems rebellion against Allah's authority.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) says the wealthy pay Zakat to the state, which provides for the needy.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) lists the Qur'anic "limitation in connection with the plurality of" wives among laws that can never be transgressed, so more than one wife is allowed within that limit.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (chs. 1, 4) holds that the legislature may legislate only within the limits of the Qur'an and Sunnah, so no parliament is supreme.

premarital-sex.rationale: Mawdudi's Purdah has a chapter on "Punishment for Fornication", and his Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) names the Qur'anic punishment for adultery among the laws; sex outside marriage is forbidden for women and men alike.

religion-illusion.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) and Qutb's Milestones treat revelation as the true guidance and atheism and Jahiliyyah as rebellion against God; religion is not an illusion.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Purdah requires Muslim women's covering as a divine law, so a ban on religious dress is opposed.

religious-offensive-war.rationale: Qutb's Milestones (ch. 4, Jihad) says Islamic jihad is not confined to "defensive war" but aims to abolish systems that stop people accepting Allah's sovereignty, while saying Islam does not force anyone to accept its belief.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: Qutb's Milestones (ch. 4) calls jihad against oppressive systems a duty and honours those who give their lives in it.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) calls the Qur'an the word of God and the final authority above every legislature.

separate-church-state.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) criticises Western secularism ("Separation of politics from morality and religion has created more problems than it has solved") and calls the Islamic state the natural course.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Purdah grounds the differences between the sexes in nature and physiology (a chapter on "scientific facts" about woman's biology), not in social construction.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Purdah says the man "is in charge of the family" and that wife and children must obey him unless it means disobeying God, which is not equal authority.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 4) says the ruler is answerable to God and to the community; if he becomes a dictator "he assumes the character of a usurper rather than a Caliph".

spiritual-nature.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) says the Islamic state's aim is to establish virtue and eradicate evil, and that politics cut from morality and religion has brought "vulgarity in behaviour and opportunism in diplomacy".

state-harmful.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (chs. 4-6) argues for an Islamic state as the necessary vehicle of divine law; he opposes abolishing the state.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution rejects atheistic socialism and communism; Qutb's Milestones calls communist systems rebellion against God's authority.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) says the Islamic state exists to "establish virtue, eradicate evil" and to uphold and enforce the virtues Islam wants.

traditional-family.rationale: Mawdudi's Purdah (chs. on the family system) blames Western moral concepts for "the disruption of family life" and presents the family founded on marriage, with the man as provider and protector, as the base of social order.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) says in personal matters "every community is welcome to adopt its own personal law", so civil law is not uniform across religions.

universal-morality.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) and Islamic Way of Life teach that all prophets in all nations brought the same guidance and morality.

women-must-cover.rationale: Mawdudi's Purdah (chapter "Covering the Face") says "the Islamic Shari'ah enjoins on the woman to hide her face from the other people" and treats Purdah as divine law, not custom; Islamic Law and Constitution (ch. 1) describes the Islamic society as one where painted women do not appear in public.

women-suffrage.rationale: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution (proposals for the constitution, ch. 10) wants women's vote qualified by an education standard and calls women's election to legislatures "absolutely against the spirit and precepts of Islam", since active politics and administration are "not the field of activity of the womenfolk".

notes: Later pass on the primary texts: Mawdudi's Islamic Law and Constitution, Purdah and Islamic Way of Life, and Qutb's Milestones, searched for state and sovereignty, clerical rule, elections and dictatorship, women and dress, family, economy (interest, Zakat, property, equality), minorities and personal law, nationalism, socialism and communism, penal law, jihad. Answers rest on these texts only; the committed answers that rested on Wikipedia or on inference are null unless these texts state the position. Silent on apostasy, blasphemy, homosexuality and abortion in the texts read. Fundamentalists and Islamists overlap heavily; Quietist Salafis and Khomeinist clerical rulers would answer clerical-rule, monarchy and violence differently.
